lessons.title: Promise chains and error propagation
lessons.summary: Complete transformed: return a chain that doubles value, recovers any thrown error here to -1, and appends cleanup exactly once in finally. Inputs are a number, Boolean fail flag and mutable events array.
explanation: then(onFulfilled) returns a new Promise. A returned value fulfills that next promise; a thrown error rejects it. Returning another promise makes the chain wait for that promise. Promise.resolve(value) supplies the initial fulfilled promise here. Callbacks run after the current synchronous work, not inside the call to then.

catch(onRejected) handles rejection and returns a new promise. Returning -1 recovers with that value; throwing would continue rejection. finally(onFinally) runs on either outcome without receiving the value/error. A normal return from finally does not replace the prior outcome, but throwing or returning a rejected promise from it can replace it.

explanation: Promise.all(iterable) returns a promise for an array of fulfilled values in input order. If an input rejects, the result rejects with a rejection reason; this does not cancel the other operations. It is useful when every result is needed.

Promise.allSettled(iterable) waits until every input settles and fulfills with records in input order. A fulfilled record has status and value; a rejected record has status and reason. It does not turn a failed operation into a successful one: it preserves the failure as data.

The result arrays follow input order, not whichever operation happens to finish first. Empty input produces an empty array. Optional practice: reverse the two supplied promises and predict the returned record order before running.

lessons.title: Timers and cancellation
lessons.summary: Complete timerLabels(label): cancel the first scheduled callback using its handle, let the second append label, and return its completion promise. Do not use busy waiting or assert an exact elapsed duration.
explanation: setTimeout(callback, delay) schedules a callback for later and returns a host-specific handle. The delay is a minimum scheduling request in milliseconds, not an exact appointment or a pause in the current function. A zero delay still waits until the current synchronous work finishes. Browsers and Node provide this host API; it is not an ECMAScript language timer.

clearTimeout(handle) cancels that pending timer and returns undefined. It does not undo a callback that already ran. Keep the handle instead of trying to cancel by callback name. The first timer below is cancelled synchronously, before it can run.

The cancelled callback contributes no entry. The other callback appends the supplied label and completes the promise. Optional practice: change that label and predict the output; do not infer a precise delay or benchmark from it. Repeated scheduling needs an explicit lifetime/cleanup design rather than abandoned timers.

lessons.title: Custom iterable protocol
lessons.summary: Complete countdown(start) so each Symbol.iterator call creates a fresh descending iterator. next returns positive values down to one, then done:true forever. Inputs are small nonnegative integers.
explanation: An object is iterable when its [Symbol.iterator] method returns an iterator. The brackets compute the method key from the well-known Symbol; this is not a newly invented Symbol("iterator"). for...of calls that method and repeatedly asks the returned iterator for its next item.

iterator.next() returns an object with value and done. done:false supplies another item; done:true marks completion. The current-- expression returns the old counter then decreases it. Our iterator keeps returning done:true after exhaustion. Each new Symbol.iterator call gets a fresh counter, so this iterable can start again.

Reusing one exhausted iterator does not restart it. Asking this iterable for another iterator does. Optional practice: obtain two iterators and advance one without changing the other; neither owns an external resource in this bounded example.

lessons.title: AbortController signal behavior
lessons.summary: Complete waitForAbort(signal): reject with signal.reason immediately if already aborted, otherwise reject on its next abort event with a once listener. Do not resolve on cancellation or start network work.
explanation: new AbortController() creates a controller with a signal. controller.abort(reason) marks that signal aborted, stores its reason and dispatches its abort event. It returns undefined. The signal is one-shot: a later abort does not reset it or replace the first reason. This is a host API, not a forced interruption of arbitrary JavaScript.

waitForAbort(signal) returns a promise that rejects with the signal’s reason. Check signal.aborted before listening, because an earlier abort will not replay its event for a new listener. Otherwise addEventListener("abort", callback, {once:true}) registers one callback that is removed after its first invocation.

Calling waitForAbort after abort still rejects immediately through its initial check. Optional practice: abort twice with different reasons and explain why the first remains. A real operation must observe its signal and release its own resources; merely creating an AbortController does not cancel unrelated work.

lessons.summary: Complete readTopic(response): return HTTP:status for a non-ok response without reading it; otherwise await json, require a non-null object with a String topic, and return that topic. Preserve parse errors and throw TypeError for the wrong shape. No fetch is needed.
explanation: new Response(body, options) constructs a local response with the supplied body, status and headers. It does not call fetch or contact a server. response.ok is true for statuses 200 through 299; status exposes the actual code. A response with status 404 is still a response object, not automatically a thrown transport error.

response.json() takes no arguments and returns a Promise for the parsed body value. It consumes the body; bodyUsed records that use. A second read of this consumed body rejects with TypeError. Malformed JSON rejects with SyntaxError, while valid JSON can still have the wrong shape. The Content-Type header does not enforce our application’s topic field.
